title: What are the producer partitioning strategies (round-robin when no key, hash-of-key for ordering per key, custom `Partitioner`), and how does each affect ordering and load distribution?
shortTitle: Producer partitioning strategies (round-robin, hash-of-key, custom) and their effect on ordering and load

s1_definition.profdef: A producer partitioning strategy decides which partition each record is written to. When a record has no key, the default partitioner uses a sticky or round-robin approach that spreads records evenly for maximum throughput but provides no per-entity ordering. When a record has a key, the partitioner hashes the key modulo the partition count, so records with the same key always go to the same partition and are ordered relative to each other. A custom `Partitioner` lets you override this with business logic, for example routing by account tier. Each strategy trades ordering against load distribution differently.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India directing customers to teller windows. Round-robin with no key is like a greeter who just sends the next customer to whichever window is free, which keeps all windows busy but means one customer's two visits might go to different windows in any order. Hash-of-key is like saying every customer always goes to the window matching the last digit of their account, so one account's transactions are always handled in order at the same window. A custom partitioner is like a VIP rule: premium accounts always go to a dedicated express window. Each rule changes how even the queues are and whether one customer's actions stay in order.
s1_definition.oneliner: No key means round-robin for even load but no ordering; a key means hash-of-key for per-key ordering; a custom partitioner lets business rules decide, trading off ordering and balance.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A producer partitioning strategy decides which partition each record is written to. When a record has no key, the default partitioner uses a sticky or round-robin approach that spreads records evenly for maximum throughput but provides no per-entity ordering. When a record has a key, the partitioner hashes the key modulo the partition count, so records with the same key always go to the same partition and are ordered relative to each other. A custom `Partitioner` lets you override this with business logic, for example routing by account tier. Each strategy trades ordering against load distribution differently.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India directing customers to teller windows. Round-robin with no key is like a greeter who just sends the next customer to whichever window is free, which keeps all windows busy but means one customer's two visits might go to different windows in any order. Hash-of-key is like saying every customer always goes to the window matching the last digit of their account, so one account's transactions are always handled in order at the same window. A custom partitioner is like a VIP rule: premium accounts always go to a dedicated express window. Each rule changes how even the queues are and whether one customer's actions stay in order.

**One line to remember:** No key means round-robin for even load but no ordering; a key means hash-of-key for per-key ordering; a custom partitioner lets business rules decide, trading off ordering and balance.

sections.s2_technical:
When you send a record with a null key, modern Kafka uses the sticky partitioner. It fills one partition for a batch, then switches to another, which keeps batches full and throughput high while still spreading records across partitions over time. The older behaviour was strict round-robin per record. Either way, with no key there is no guarantee about the order of two related records, because they may land in different partitions, and order is only guaranteed within a single partition. This strategy is ideal for independent events like clickstream or log lines where ordering between items does not matter.

When you send a record with a key, the default partitioner computes `murmur2(key) % numPartitions`. The same key always maps to the same partition, so all records for that key are ordered. In a bank you key by account id so that for a given account, a debit written before a credit is also consumed before that credit. The cost is that distribution is only as even as the key's cardinality and skew, which is why key choice matters.

A custom `Partitioner` implements the `partition` method and can apply any logic. For example, you might send premium or high-volume merchant accounts to a reserved set of partitions so they get dedicated consumer capacity, while routing everyone else with the normal hash. In code you implement `org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Partitioner` and configure it with `props.put(ProducerConfig.PARTITIONER_CLASS_CONFIG, TierPartitioner.class.getName())`. You can also bypass the partitioner entirely by passing an explicit partition number to the `ProducerRecord`, which you use rarely and carefully.

The senior nuances are these. Ordering is always only within a partition, never across partitions, so the only way to get global ordering is a single partition, which destroys parallelism. Keying for ordering and keeping load even are in tension, so you pick the key that satisfies your ordering requirement first, then address skew. Changing the partition count later rehashes keys, so records for a key can move to a different partition and ordering across the change boundary is not preserved for in-flight data. A custom partitioner is powerful but becomes a piece of code you must test and maintain, so I use it only when the default plus a good key cannot express the requirement.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India emits two kinds of events. Audit log lines are independent and only need high throughput, so they are produced with no key. This is exactly the round-robin or sticky case — spread evenly, ordering between lines does not matter.

Problem 2 — Transfer events for a single account must be processed in order, because a credit must not be applied before the matching debit. These are produced with the account id as the key. This is exactly the hash-of-key case — same account, same partition, ordered.

Problem 3 — Premium corporate accounts need guaranteed capacity so their settlement is never stuck behind retail traffic. A custom partitioner routes premium accounts to a dedicated partition range. This is exactly the custom `Partitioner` case — business logic overrides the default hash.

We demonstrate all three strategies in plain Java with a `PartitionStrategy` interface and three implementations, then route a mixed batch and print where each record lands. The code will show: the `Event` model, a `RoundRobinStrategy`, a `HashKeyStrategy`, a `TierPartitioner`, and a demo showing ordering and distribution for each.

```yaml
# application.yml — configure a custom partitioner in a real producer
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    producer:
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonSerializer
      properties:
        partitioner.class: com.bank.strategy.strategy.TierPartitioner
        partitioner.premium.partitions: "10,11"   # dedicated for premium
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five events — two keyless audit lines, two transfers for SAV2001, one premium transfer for CUR3001.

Step 1: Under the round-robin strategy, the two audit events go to partitions chosen by a rotating counter, for example partition 0 then partition 1. They spread evenly, and there is no ordering relationship enforced between them.

Step 2: Still under round-robin, the transfer events also rotate across partitions, so SAV2001's two transfers could land on different partitions. That means their order is not guaranteed, which would be wrong for a bank, so round-robin is only used for the independent audit events.

Step 3: Under the hash-of-key strategy, SAV2001 hashes to one fixed partition, so both of its transfers land on the same partition and are therefore consumed in the order they were produced. CUR3001 hashes to its own partition.

Step 4: Under the custom tier partitioner, the premium CUR3001 transfer is routed to partition 10 or 11, which are reserved for premium traffic, so it gets dedicated consumer capacity. Retail accounts are hashed only over partitions 0 through 9.

Step 5: The demo prints each placement, making it clear that SAV2001's two transfers share one partition under hashing, and that premium traffic is isolated under the custom partitioner.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Producer send(event)
    │
    ├─ no key ─────────→ Sticky/RoundRobin ─→ P0,P1,P2...  even load, NO ordering
    │
    ├─ key=accountId ──→ hash(key) % 12 ────→ same acc → same P → ORDERED per account
    │
    └─ premium flag ───→ TierPartitioner ───→ premium → P10/P11 (dedicated)
                                              retail  → P0..P9
    ▼
  Kafka topic "events" (12 partitions)
    │
    ▼
  Consumer group: ordering preserved within each partition only
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
There are three producer partitioning strategies, and each makes a different trade-off between ordering and load distribution. When a record has no key, Kafka uses the sticky or round-robin partitioner, which fills batches efficiently and spreads records evenly across partitions for maximum throughput, but it provides no ordering between related records because they can land on different partitions. I use this for truly independent events like audit log lines, where the order between items does not matter.

When a record has a key, the default partitioner hashes the key modulo the partition count, so the same key always maps to the same partition. That gives me per-key ordering, which is exactly what a bank needs: by keying transfer events on account id, every event for one account lands on one partition and is consumed in the order it was produced, so a credit is never applied before its matching debit. The cost is that distribution is only as even as the key's cardinality, so a skewed key creates a hot partition.

A custom partitioner lets business logic override the default. I implement Kafka's Partitioner interface and configure it through the partitioner class property. A realistic banking use is routing premium or high-volume corporate accounts to a dedicated set of partitions so their settlement gets guaranteed consumer capacity and is never stuck behind retail traffic. The nuance I always state is that ordering is only ever guaranteed within a partition, never across partitions, so global ordering would require a single partition and would kill parallelism, and that changing the partition count later rehashes keys and can move a key to a new partition.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, we use all three. Audit events are keyless and round-robin for throughput, transfer events are keyed by account id for strict per-account ordering, and we wrote a custom tier partitioner that sends premium corporate accounts to two reserved partitions with their own dedicated consumers so their service level is protected. The senior framing I give is that partitioning is where you encode both your correctness requirement, which is ordering, and your performance requirement, which is balance, so I always decide the ordering need first, pick the key that satisfies it, and only reach for a custom partitioner when the default plus a good key cannot express the business rule.
